newsitem.title: MOLDOVA: Moldova, Dnestr separatists resolve differences.
newsitem.headline: Moldova, Dnestr separatists resolve differences.

text.p: Moldova and its separatist Dnestr region have made a breakthrough that paves the way to ending their conflict, Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov said on Friday.

Primakov, who mediated talks between President Petru Lucinschi and Dnestr separatist leader Igor Smirnov, said the two sides had resolved months of differences which had held up the signing of a memorandum to normalise ties.
"A breakthrough has been made in relations between Moldova and Dnestr," Primakov told a joint news conference with Moldovan Foreign Minister Mihai Popov in the Moldovan capital Chisinau.
He said the memorandum would be signed in Moscow by May 15.

Security forces of Moldova, a former Soviet republic in which most people speak a Latin language related to that of neighbouring Romania, clashed in 1992 with separatists demanding independence for the Russian- and Ukrainian-speaking people of Dnestr, an eastern region which is the country's industrial heartland.
Hundreds of people were killed before Russian peacekeeping troops intervened.

A memorandum setting out the terms for normalising ties was worked out last summer. But Lucinschi had said he would sign it only if it was altered to respect the former Soviet republic's territorial integrity.

A representative of the Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe also criticised the memorandum after it was drafted last June, saying its provisions did not reaffirm the OSCE principles of sovereignty and territorial integrity.

Primakov said an article had now been added to the memorandum committing the sides to "relations within the framework of a common state and within the framework of (the former) Moldavian Soviet Socialist Republic's borders as of January 1990".
"This article has removed the blocks to the memorandum", Primakov said, explaining that January 1990 preceded Dnestr's declaration of independence.
Popov said the two sides would start work on a "wide-ranging document defining the status of the Dnestr region within the Republic of Moldova" after the memorandum is signed.
Russia still has up to 6,000 peacekeepers in Dnestr, a region of about 700,000 people, and regards stability there and in other parts of the former Soviet Union as vital for its own security.
"Russia has the greatest interest in the stabilisation of the situation in the region," Primakov said.

Popov said relations with Moscow were also vital for Moldova. "Russia is the most important stategic partner for Russia and Chisinau and Moscow would like our relations to develop naturally," he told the news conference.

Primakov said Moscow would eventually withdraw its troops but did not say when. Moldova and Russia signed an agreement in 1994 to withdraw the troops within three years, but it was never ratified by the Russian State Duma lower house of parliament.
